title: Evaluating Twitter's algorithmic amplification of low-credibility content: an observational study
screen_reason: Observational study of ~2.7m COVID-19 and climate-change tweets collected from the Twitter API (15-29 Jan 2023). It reports the share of tweets in each topical corpus that carry a URL from a low-credibility domain (3.77% COVID-19; 1.69% climate change), i.e. a quantitative prevalence with a stated denominator. The amplification analysis itself (bootstrapped impression differences) is not a prevalence share and yields no rows.

estimates.measure_type: % of original tweets in the COVID-19 keyword corpus that contain a URL from a low-credibility domain
estimates.value_raw: low-credibility domains present in 3.77% of tweets on COVID-19
estimates.denominator: approximately 2.1 million original English-language tweets on COVID-19 (retweets excluded) collected from the Twitter API v2 over 15-29 Jan 2023
estimates.definition: the tweet contains a URL whose domain has an aggregate credibility score <= 0.4 in the Lin et al. (2023) aggregated domain-rating set
estimates.misinfo_def: "tweets with a credibility score lower or equal to 0.4 to be low-credibility"; low-credibility content is used as "a baseline for false or misleading information"
estimates.source_quote:
This process results

19 and 1.69% of tweets on climate change.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: aggregate domain reliability scores for 11,520 domains from Lin et al. (2023, PNAS Nexus), built by principal component analysis over the major existing rating sets; cut-offs <=0.4 low-credibility, >=0.6 high-credibility, chosen 'in line with the values used by major credibility ratings providers such as Newsguard'. No reliability statistics reported for the tweet-level assignment.

estimates.notes: Judgement call for an adjudicator: the denominator is every original tweet in the topical keyword corpus (retweets are explicitly excluded), not the set of shared/reshared items, so this is coded CONTENT under the denominator rule ('all items that exist'). A reading of 'tweets sharing information from low-credibility domains' as SHARING/content_share is defensible but would need a denominator of shared items, which the paper does not use. Denominator size is the paper's own approximation (~2.1m); the exact count is not printed.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: (a) the amplification results (+19.2% COVID-19, +95.8% climate change mean impression difference; +30.2% / +129% in stratum 3,3; toxicity +9.9/+15.2; right-leaning +6/+24.3; verified +155%/+138%) - these are relative differences in impressions between low- and high-credibility samples, not a share of anything with a misinformation numerator, so they carry no prevalence estimate. (b) 87,769 low-credibility vs 187,643 high-credibility tweets pooled across both datasets: a pooled share (87,769/2.7m) would be a cross-category computation the paper never states, so it is not kept under R8. (c) '5596 political domains - around 10% of all domains in the data' is a share of political, not low-credibility, domains. (d) Table 1 gives per-domain tweet frequencies but no denominator-based share. No CONCENTRATION estimate is reported: the paper says high-engagement tweets generate most impressions but gives no top-X% / share-of-Y pair.

rob.design: Observational digital-trace study; English-language keyword collection from the Twitter API v2 over a fixed 14-day window (15-29 Jan 2023), ~2.1m COVID-19 and ~600k climate-change original tweets (retweets excluded); no sampling of users, so no response rate. Misinformation coded automatically at the source level from an external aggregate domain-credibility score set (Lin et al. 2023, 11,520 domains) at fixed cut-offs (<=0.4 / >=0.6); no human coding and no inter-coder reliability for the credibility assignment. Auxiliary GPT-4 political-bias labels were validated against Media Bias/Fact Check on the 20 most common domains with 95% agreement in macro political areas; verified status validated on 20+20 accounts. Single author, single platform, single-language keyword frame; results limited to tweets carrying URLs.
